blocks.text: 1. Tokenization

blocks.alt: Raw text goes through a tokenizer to produce tokens

blocks.text: The Generative Models module, already covered across this course, closed with autoregressive generation. Tokenization, the process of splitting raw text into the discrete pieces a model actually operates on, is the natural place to begin looking at how language models actually work.
This topic genuinely opens this course's own Large Language Models module, the foundational first step behind everything else covered throughout it.
2. Raw Text Is Not Directly Usable
This connects back to a neural network needing numeric input, already covered generally across this course. Raw text is genuinely just a sequence of characters, not numbers a network can process.
Something genuinely has to convert that text into a fixed set of discrete units first, a genuinely necessary first step explored throughout the rest of this topic.
3. What A Token Is

blocks.alt: A token maps to a token ID

blocks.text: This connects back to raw text not being directly usable, already covered in this topic. A token is genuinely one of those discrete units: a word, part of a word, or even a single character.
Every genuinely tokenizer defines its own exact rules for where those unit boundaries fall, a genuinely important design choice explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.text: 4. Word Level Splitting

blocks.alt: A sentence splits into whole word tokens

blocks.text: This connects back to what a token is, already covered in this topic. The genuinely simplest scheme splits text on whitespace and punctuation into whole words.
This is genuinely simple, but it genuinely produces a huge vocabulary and struggles with unseen words, a genuinely real limitation explored throughout the rest of this topic.
5. Character Level Splitting

blocks.alt: A word splits into individual character tokens

blocks.text: This connects back to word level splitting, already covered in this topic. An alternative genuinely splits text down to individual characters instead of whole words.
This produces a genuinely tiny vocabulary, but genuinely very long sequences for the exact same piece of text, a genuinely opposite tradeoff explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This tradeoff, already covered in this topic, directly motivates Subword Tokenization, covered as the next topic in this module, which genuinely sits between these two extremes.

blocks.text: 6. The Vocabulary And Token IDs

blocks.alt: A token is looked up in the vocabulary to produce a token ID

blocks.text: This connects back to word level and character level splitting, already covered in this topic. Every genuinely possible token gets assigned one fixed integer ID inside a vocabulary.
The model genuinely only ever sees those integer IDs, never the raw text itself, a genuinely important detail explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This integer ID mapping, already covered in this topic, directly sets up Vocabulary, covered as a later topic in this module, which explores exactly how that fixed set of tokens is chosen and sized.

blocks.text: 7. Tokenization Before Embeddings

blocks.alt: Raw text goes through tokenization before embeddings

blocks.text: This connects back to token IDs, already covered in this topic. Those genuinely integer token IDs then feed directly into an embedding lookup, already covered generally in Word Embeddings.
Tokenization genuinely has to happen first, before any embedding or attention computation can even begin, the genuinely necessary starting point of the entire modeling pipeline.

blocks.text: 8. Tokenization Affects Sequence Length
This connects back to tokenization happening first, already covered in this topic. Genuinely how text gets split directly determines how many tokens a given passage becomes.
This genuinely matters directly for the context window, covered as a later topic in this module, a genuinely real, practical consequence of the tokenization scheme chosen.
9. Recognizing Why Tokenization Is Genuinely A Foundational First Step

blocks.alt: Feeding text to a model points toward needing tokenization first

blocks.text: This connects back to raw text not being directly usable, already covered in this topic. Tokenization, already covered in this topic, directly solves exactly that problem.

This connects back to word level splitting's own vocabulary and unseen-word problems, already covered in this topic. Subword Tokenization, covered as the next topic in this module, genuinely addresses exactly those problems.
10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates a simple word level tokenizer, already covered in this topic, converting text into token IDs.

code.content:
import re

def word_tokenize(text):
    # already covered as word level splitting in this topic
    return re.findall(r"[a-zA-Z']+|[.,!?;]", text.lower())

def build_vocabulary(tokens):
    # already covered as the vocabulary and token IDs in this topic
    unique_tokens = sorted(set(tokens))
    return {token: idx for idx, token in enumerate(unique_tokens)}

text = "The cat sat on the mat. The cat ran."

tokens = word_tokenize(text)
print(f"Tokens (already covered as word level splitting in this topic): {tokens}")

vocabulary = build_vocabulary(tokens)
print(f"\nVocabulary (already covered in this topic): {vocabulary}")

token_ids = [vocabulary[t] for t in tokens]
print(f"\nToken IDs (already covered in this topic): {token_ids}")
print(f"\nSequence length (already covered in this topic): {len(token_ids)} tokens")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows raw text becoming a fixed sequence of integer token IDs, exactly the mechanism already covered in this topic, with repeated words like "the" and "cat" correctly reusing the exact same ID.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Tokenization splits raw text into the discrete pieces, tokens, a model actually operates on.
Neural networks need numeric input, so raw text must be converted into discrete units first.
A token can be a whole word, part of a word, or a single character, depending on the scheme.
Word level splitting is simple but produces a huge vocabulary and struggles with unseen words.
Character level splitting produces a tiny vocabulary but much longer sequences.
Every token in the vocabulary gets a fixed integer ID; the model only ever sees those IDs.
Tokenization happens before embedding lookup, feeding token IDs into the rest of the pipeline.
How text is tokenized directly determines how many tokens a passage becomes, affecting context window usage.
Next up: Subword Tokenization, a scheme sitting between whole words and individual characters.
